title: CLoVE: Finding Client Clusters Using Loss Patterns
one_liner: CLoVE discovers which clients belong together by watching how much each client's data breaks different models.
lead: In federated learning, you train a shared model on thousands of devices without seeing their private data. But different devices have different kinds of data. CLoVE discovers which devices have similar data by looking at a simple signal: how much each client's data breaks a candidate model (the loss). Clients in the same group will break models the same way; clients in different groups break them differently.

problem.h2: Clustering clients in federated learning is invisible
paras: In federated learning, a central server sends a model to thousands of personal devices — phones, computers, wearables. Each device trains the model on its own private data without sending the raw data back. This privacy is the whole point. But there's a catch: not all devices have the same kind of data. A phone in New York has different pictures and typing patterns than a phone in Tokyo. If you train a single global model, it becomes a weak compromise that fits no one well.

The natural idea is to train cluster-specific models: one cluster handles New York phones, another handles Tokyo phones. But the server cannot see the device data, so it cannot figure out which devices belong to which cluster. A naive first try: watch which model each device trains best on, and assign it there. But this breaks when two clusters share a weak spot on the same model — both get assigned to it, and the true clustering collapses into garbage. The server gets no signal to correct this.

callout.html: CLoVE assigns devices to clusters by analyzing how much each device's data breaks each candidate model, because devices in the same true cluster will break models in the same characteristic pattern.

panels.title: 1. The setup: devices with hidden clusters
panels.caption: A server sends model down to thousands of devices. Devices in blue group have similar data; red group has different data.

panels.title: 2. Naive method: assign to best model
panels.caption: All devices check both models A and B. Blue-group devices break model B worst; red-group devices break model A worst. But both point to model B.

panels.title: 3. The problem: assignment collides
panels.caption: If both groups find model B the worst fit, they both get assigned there. The clustering is lost. Model A never gets updated.

panels.title: 4. CLoVE uses loss patterns instead
panels.viz_args: Device 1: [85, 30] vs Device 2: [88, 32] — different pairs, different clusters
panels.caption: Don't just pick the worst model. Look at the whole pattern: all losses across all models. Devices in the same cluster have similar patterns.

panels.title: 5. Clustering recovers the true groups
panels.caption: Group devices by comparing their loss patterns. Devices with similar patterns cluster together, revealing the true structure.

steps.text: Start with K candidate models (guessing how many clusters exist). Server sends them to all devices.
Each device runs its private data through all K models, records how much each model fails on that data.
Send loss patterns to server. Server groups devices whose loss patterns are similar (e.g. via k-means).
For each cluster, aggregate the model updates from only the devices in that cluster.
Stop re-clustering once device assignments stop changing. Then reuse the cluster models for new devices.

paras: CLoVE changes how the server assigns devices to clusters. Instead of watching which single model performs best (which can collapse), it watches the full pattern of losses across all candidate models. This pattern is a list: Device A might have [loss on model 1, loss on model 2, loss on model 3] = [85, 30, 72]. Device B might have [88, 32, 75]. These patterns look similar because the two devices have similar data, so they cluster together.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: loss pattern similarity
hidden.name: Loss-pattern distance between devices
paras: The paper measures something the server can never see directly: which devices truly have similar data. It infers this from loss patterns. The core insight is this: if two devices break the same set of models in the same characteristic way (e.g. both fail worst on model 2, both do okay on model 1), then they likely have similar data and belong in the same cluster. Conversely, if device A breaks models in one pattern and device B in a completely different pattern, they belong in different clusters.

The paper estimates this similarity by computing how far apart loss patterns are. Two devices are close if their loss patterns are similar (measured by the straight-line distance between the two lists of numbers). Devices that are close get clustered together. The server never needs to see the raw data — just these loss patterns suffice to infer the true clustering.

heat.caption: Darker loss means that device's data breaks that model badly. Notice: A and B have the same pattern (high in model 1, low in model 2), so they cluster. C and D share a different pattern, so they form a second cluster.

reads.html: Devices with similar loss patterns have similar data and should train together.
The loss pattern encoding infers cluster membership by grouping devices whose losses are similar, measured from the data collected from each device for each candidate model.

mechanism.h2: Why loss patterns reveal true clusters
paras: Here is the mechanical core: when two devices have genuinely similar data (like two phones in the same city with the same regional app usage patterns), any given model will perform in a similar way on both devices. If model A is good at recognizing handwriting with that city's accent, it will do well on both devices. If model B was trained on a different accent, it will do poorly on both devices. The devices' loss patterns will align.

In contrast, if two devices have very different data (one from the city, one from the countryside), a model trained for city data will perform well on one and poorly on the other. Their loss patterns will diverge. By comparing loss patterns across all candidate models, the server gets a detailed signature of each device's data without ever seeing the data itself. Devices whose signatures cluster together truly belong together, because they behave the same way across the full model lineup.

This is fundamentally different from watching a single loss value (the naive approach). A single value is too coarse. But a loss pattern across multiple models is fine-grained (it tells you loss on model A, loss on model B, loss on model C...). It captures which models are good fits and which are bad fits, painting a portrait of the data's structure. Devices with the same portrait have the same underlying data, and thus belong in the same cluster.

stages.s: Device sends: 'I ran my data through models A, B, C. Got losses [85, 30, 72].'
Server collects loss patterns from all devices in current round.
Server groups devices by loss-vector distance (e.g. devices with [85, 30, 72] near [88, 32, 75] form a cluster).
For each cluster, update its model with only the devices in that cluster.
Cluster assignments converge; specialized models trained; new devices assigned by nearest centroid.

math.words: For each device, form a loss vector by running the device's data through each candidate model. Cluster devices by grouping together those whose loss vectors are close in distance. The clustering can be done by k-means: compute the centroid of each group, then assign each device to the nearest centroid.
math.equation: d_i = [loss_i_model_1, loss_i_model_2, ..., loss_i_model_K] ; cluster_j = {i : argmin_k ||d_i - centroid_k|| = j}
symbols: loss vector for device i: a list of losses on all K candidate models
measured loss (error) when device i runs its data through model k
the average loss vector of all devices assigned to cluster k
distance between device i's loss vector and cluster k's center

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Device 1 loss vector: [85, 30, 72] (it breaks model 1 badly, model 2 okay, model 3 poorly).
D1 and D2 are close (distance 4.7), so they cluster together. D3 is far away (distance 86.6), so it goes to a different cluster.

math.note: Devices with similar loss patterns are close in the loss-vector space, so they cluster together and train specialized models.

items.html: If you guess there are 3 clusters but there are really 5, the loss vectors won't separate into the true clusters. CLoVE uses a clustering quality score to detect this and re-estimate the true number, but this adds communication rounds.

If devices have very little data, their loss measurements are noisy (unstable). Noisy patterns can be hard to cluster reliably, because the distance between two similar devices might be dominated by random fluctuations rather than true data differences. Collecting more device data per round helps, because more data produces stabler loss measurements that reveal the true underlying pattern.
Some devices may not finish computing all K model losses. If a device sends an incomplete loss vector, its cluster assignment becomes unreliable.

CLoVE assumes loss patterns are stable (devices run the same models, collect enough samples), and that the true number of clusters can be roughly guessed. Under these conditions, cluster recovery happens in a handful of rounds.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small federated learning setup with 10 simulated devices split into two true clusters (cluster A has devices 1-5 with similar handwritten-digit data; cluster B has devices 6-10 with similar rotated-digit data). Initialize two candidate models. Run CLoVE for 5 rounds. At the end, measure two things: (1) How accurately did CLoVE recover the true clusters? Print a confusion matrix of assigned vs. true clusters. (2) How well did each cluster-specific model fit its cluster? Print the final accuracy of Model 1 on cluster A and Model 2 on cluster B, and compare to a baseline where both models are trained on all devices mixed.
demo.metric_eq: cluster_recovery_accuracy = (number of devices assigned to correct cluster) / (total devices) ; cluster_A_model_accuracy = accuracy of model A on test data from cluster A devices
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss: loss-pattern clustering recovers the true clusters faster than naive assignment because it uses the full pattern rather than a single value, and specialized models outperform the mixed baseline because each model can optimize for its own cluster's unique data instead of compromising to fit everyone.
